nodes.title: Cloud fundamentals: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Every cloud certification starts with the same vocabulary: IaaS / PaaS / SaaS, public / private / hybrid, capex vs opex, elasticity, regions and AZs. Getting these right is half the foundational exam.

flashcards.front: IaaS vs PaaS vs SaaS — pick an example of each.
flashcards.back: IaaS (Infrastructure): EC2, Azure VM, Compute Engine — you manage OS and up. PaaS (Platform): App Engine, Elastic Beanstalk, App Service — you manage code, provider manages runtime. SaaS (Software): Gmail, Salesforce — you just use it. As you go up the stack, you get convenience, lose control.

flashcards.front: Region vs Availability Zone — what's the difference?
flashcards.back: A region is a geographic area (us-east-1, europe-west2). An AZ is one or more data centers inside a region with independent power/cooling/network. AZs in a region are connected by low-latency fiber but isolated from each other's failures. Best practice: spread workload across 2-3 AZs for HA.

Scalability: the system can be grown (add capacity to handle 10x load). Elasticity: it auto-shrinks back when load drops — you don't pay for idle capacity. A scalable system isn't necessarily elastic (a manually-resized DB is scalable but not elastic). Cloud's killer feature is being both.

flashcards.front: Capex vs opex — why does cloud favor opex?
flashcards.back: Capex (capital expenditure): big upfront purchase (a server, a building). Opex (operating expenditure): ongoing per-unit cost (cloud usage, electricity). Cloud turns infrastructure into opex — no $500k server purchases, just monthly bills. Easier for finance to scale, easier to abandon a project without sunk cost.

questions.q: A company migrates its email and collaboration workloads to a SaaS platform. Under the cloud shared responsibility model, who is responsible for patching the underlying server operating system?
choices: The cloud customer, since they retain administrative control over the platform's application deployment — in a SaaS model the customer has no control over the underlying application, runtime, or OS patching; those responsibilities belong entirely to the cloud provider
The cloud provider, since the provider operates the application, runtime, OS, and hardware in a SaaS model
The cloud customer, since guest operating system patching is a customer duty under the IaaS responsibility split
A contracted cloud broker, since brokers assume the infrastructure maintenance duties on behalf of SaaS tenants
questions.explanation: In the shared responsibility model the split of duties shifts with the service model. For SaaS, the provider operates the entire stack — application, runtime, guest OS, virtualization, and physical hardware — while the customer is responsible mainly for its data, user identities, and the application settings exposed to it. Guest-OS patching becomes a customer duty only under IaaS. A cloud broker intermediates service delivery and does not assume infrastructure maintenance.

questions.q: A finance team provisions additional virtual machines through a self-service portal at any hour, with no need to contact provider staff. Which NIST essential characteristic of cloud computing does this describe?
choices: Rapid elasticity — capacity scales outward and inward to track changing demand — rapid elasticity describes automatic scaling of resources that the cloud self-provisions and de-provisions; it does not describe a consumer who provisions computing capacity unilaterally without provider interaction
Resource pooling — provider resources serve multiple consumers through a multitenant model
On-demand self-service — a consumer provisions computing capacity unilaterally as it is needed
Measured service — resource usage is metered, controlled, and reported back for transparency
questions.explanation: NIST SP 800-145 defines five essential characteristics. On-demand self-service means a consumer can unilaterally provision capabilities such as compute and storage automatically, without human interaction with the provider — exactly the 'no need to contact staff' trait highlighted here. Rapid elasticity concerns automatic scaling to demand, resource pooling concerns multitenancy, and measured service concerns metering and billing.

questions.q: At which phase of the cloud data lifecycle should data be classified and assigned access rights, so that appropriate protection is inherited through every later phase?
choices: Create — labeling data as it originates lets controls travel with it through all later phases

Store — applying controls once data is committed to persistent storage protects at-rest data but does not enforce classification during earlier lifecycle phases, and labels applied later may travel through the Create and Use phases without controls
Use — classifying at the point of processing reflects how the data is actually being consumed
Archive — labeling data before long-term retention aligns handling with disposal requirements
questions.explanation: The cloud data lifecycle runs Create, Store, Use, Share, Archive, Destroy. Classification and the assignment of access rights belong in the Create phase, the moment data originates, so every later phase inherits the right protection. Deferring classification to Store, Use, or Archive leaves intervals in which the data is unclassified and inadequately protected.

questions.q: A retailer wants its cloud application database to stop holding actual primary account numbers (PANs) while still referencing each card consistently for refunds. Which technique BEST meets this need?
choices: Transparent encryption — the PAN is stored as ciphertext while the application still reads plaintext
Data masking — PAN digits are replaced with fixed characters so only the last four stay visible
Hashing — the PAN is converted to a fixed-length digest from which the value cannot be recovered
Tokenization — the PAN is replaced with a non-sensitive surrogate mapped in a separate secure vault
questions.explanation: Tokenization swaps a sensitive value for a non-sensitive surrogate (token); the real PAN sits in a separate, strongly protected vault, so the application database never stores card numbers yet can still reference each card consistently — and it reduces PCI DSS scope. Encryption keeps a recoverable value in the database as ciphertext. Masking obscures data for display only. Hashing is one-way, which would block the consistent reversible reference refunds require.

questions.q: An attacker exploits a flaw in the virtualization layer to break out of a guest virtual machine and run code directly on the host, potentially reaching other tenants' workloads. What is this attack called?
choices: VM sprawl — unmanaged virtual machines accumulate and erode visibility — VM sprawl is a management and governance problem caused by ungoverned proliferation; it does not involve code breaking the hypervisor isolation boundary to reach the underlying host
VM rollback — a virtual machine is reverted to an earlier, less secure point-in-time snapshot
VM escape — code breaks the isolation boundary and reaches the underlying hypervisor or host
VM theft — a portable virtual machine image is copied wholesale out of the cloud environment
questions.explanation: A VM escape occurs when an attacker defeats the isolation the hypervisor enforces, executes code on the host, and can potentially affect co-located tenants — a serious multitenancy risk (full hypervisor compromise is sometimes called hyperjacking). VM sprawl is an operational governance problem, VM rollback can reintroduce removed vulnerabilities, and VM theft is exfiltration of an image file — none of which by themselves cross the guest-to-host boundary.

questions.q: Which cloud infrastructure component warrants the strictest access controls because compromising it grants broad authority over provisioning and configuration across the whole virtual environment?
choices: The management plane, which orchestrates provisioning and configuration across the environment

The guest operating system running inside one tenant's individual virtual machine — the guest OS is a tenant-controlled layer within a single VM; it does not orchestrate provisioning or manage configuration across the entire multi-tenant cloud environment
The object storage tier that holds tenant backups and infrequently accessed archive datasets
The virtual network overlay that segments east-west traffic flowing between tenant workloads
questions.explanation: The management plane is the orchestration layer used to create, configure, move, and delete virtualized resources, so its compromise is among the most damaging cloud events. It therefore warrants the strictest controls: strong MFA, least privilege, dedicated administrative accounts, and thorough logging. A single guest OS, a storage tier, or the network overlay each has a far narrower blast radius.

nodes.title: Identity and access management: Key Ideas
nodes.content: IAM is the layer that decides who can do what. It's almost always the first thing to misconfigure and the most common security failure mode. Every cloud uses the same primitives — identities, policies, roles — under slightly different names.

flashcards.front: What's the difference between authentication and authorization?
flashcards.back: Authentication (AuthN) proves who you are — password, MFA, certificate. Authorization (AuthZ) decides what you're allowed to do once authenticated — policies, roles, ACLs. AuthN happens first; AuthZ is checked on every request.

flashcards.front: What is a role (vs a user)?
flashcards.back: A user is a long-lived identity tied to a person. A role is a short-lived, assumable identity — services or users 'become' the role to get temporary credentials. Roles let you grant access without sharing long-term keys. Always prefer roles.

Identity-based policies attach to a user / role and say what THEY can do. Resource-based policies attach to a thing (S3 bucket, KMS key, SQS queue) and say who can access IT. Cross-account access usually needs both: target's resource policy says 'allow this account', source identity policy says 'allow this action on that resource'.

Instead of creating cloud users for every employee, federate from your corporate identity provider (Okta, Azure AD, Google Workspace). Users sign in once with their work account; the IdP issues a SAML / OIDC token; the cloud trades it for temporary credentials. One source of truth, instant deprovisioning.

questions.q: A SaaS provider wants enterprise customers' employees to sign in with their existing corporate credentials, without the SaaS provider ever storing those passwords. Which approach achieves this?
choices: Local account provisioning, where the SaaS application creates and stores a password for each employee
A shared service account whose single set of credentials is distributed to every employee needing access
Periodic credential synchronization that copies the corporate password hashes into the SaaS directory
Identity federation, where the SaaS application trusts authentication assertions from the customer's IdP
questions.explanation: Identity federation establishes a trust relationship in which the application (relying party) accepts authentication assertions — typically via SAML or OpenID Connect — from the customer's identity provider (IdP). The employee authenticates against their own organization, so the SaaS provider never receives or stores the password. Shared accounts destroy accountability, local provisioning forces the provider to store credentials, and synchronizing hashes still copies sensitive secrets into the SaaS environment.

questions.q: An operations team builds every new cloud server from a hardened image that disables unused services and enforces one standard secure configuration. What is this practice called?
choices: Penetration testing — actively probing a deployed system for exploitable weaknesses to find vulnerabilities before attackers do — penetration testing validates security controls after deployment; it does not establish a hardened, standard baseline configuration that every new system is built from
Baselining — deploying every system from a defined, hardened, standard secure configuration
Load balancing — distributing workload traffic across multiple servers to preserve availability, not to establish a secure baseline configuration that every system is built from
Live migration — relocating a running workload between hosts without interrupting the service
questions.explanation: Baselining establishes a documented, hardened standard configuration — minimal services, secure settings, current patches — and deploys every system from it, giving a consistent known-good posture; later deviations surface as configuration drift. Penetration testing evaluates security but does not set the standard, and load balancing and live migration are availability and operations techniques unrelated to configuration hardening.

questions.q: An enterprise wants an independent, NDA-restricted report describing both the design and the operating effectiveness of a cloud provider's security controls over a period of time, suitable for its auditors. Which report should it request?
choices: A SOC 2 Type II report, which tests control operating effectiveness across a defined reporting period

A SOC 2 Type I report, which evaluates only the design of the controls at a single point in time — Type I reports assess control design at a moment in time without testing operating effectiveness across a defined period; Type II tests effectiveness over the examination period
A SOC 1 Type II report, which covers controls relevant to financial statement reporting for clients
A SOC 3 report, which is a general-use summary that omits the detailed control testing results
questions.explanation: A SOC 2 report addresses the Trust Services Criteria (security, availability, processing integrity, confidentiality, privacy) and is restricted-use under NDA. A Type II report tests operating effectiveness across a period — commonly 6 to 12 months — which is what the auditors need. A SOC 2 Type I assesses only design at a point in time, SOC 1 focuses on controls affecting financial reporting, and SOC 3 is general-use but omits the detailed test results auditors require.

questions.q: After analysis, a cloud customer decides not to launch a planned analytics feature because the associated data-privacy risk exceeds its risk appetite. Which risk treatment option does this represent?
choices: Risk mitigation — controls are applied that reduce the likelihood or impact to an acceptable level
Risk avoidance — the risk is eliminated by choosing not to undertake the activity that creates it
Risk transfer — the financial impact of the risk is shifted to another party such as an insurer
Risk acceptance — the residual risk is formally acknowledged and the activity then proceeds anyway
questions.explanation: Risk avoidance eliminates a risk entirely by not engaging in the activity that produces it — here, cancelling the analytics feature. Risk mitigation reduces likelihood or impact through controls while still proceeding, risk transfer shifts impact to a third party such as an insurer, and risk acceptance proceeds after a documented decision to bear the residual risk. Declining to act at all is the defining trait of avoidance.

questions.q: An organization wants to enforce consistent visibility and security policy — including data loss prevention and detection of unsanctioned 'shadow IT' applications — across multiple SaaS services its employees use. Which technology is specifically designed to sit between users and cloud services to provide this?
choices: A web application firewall (WAF), which inspects HTTP requests to a single application and blocks injection and cross-site scripting attacks at that application's edge
A hardware security module (HSM), which generates and stores cryptographic keys in tamper-resistant hardware for the organization's encryption operations
A cloud access security broker (CASB), which enforces visibility, compliance, data security, and threat-protection policies between users and multiple cloud services
A bastion host, which provides a hardened, audited jump point for administrators to reach internal systems over a single controlled management channel
questions.explanation: A CASB is a policy enforcement point placed between cloud consumers and cloud providers, delivering the four pillars of visibility, compliance, data security (including DLP), and threat protection — and it is the standard tool for discovering shadow IT across many SaaS apps. A WAF protects a single web application from request-layer attacks. An HSM protects cryptographic keys. A bastion host is an administrative access gateway, not a cloud-policy broker.

questions.q: A regulated firm must encrypt cloud-stored data but, for compliance reasons, must retain sole control of the encryption keys so the cloud provider cannot decrypt the data on its own. Which key-management approach BEST satisfies this requirement?
choices: Provider-managed default encryption, in which the cloud platform automatically generates and controls the keys used to encrypt every customer object at rest
Disabling encryption and instead restricting access with IAM policies, since strong identity controls remove the need for the customer to manage any encryption keys
Storing the keys in the same managed key service the provider uses for its own internal services, so rotation and availability are handled entirely by provider automation
Customer-managed keys held in the customer's own KMS or HSM (often described as 'hold your own key'), so the provider cannot decrypt the data without the customer supplying the key
questions.explanation: Retaining sole control means the customer must own the key material — customer-managed / hold-your-own-key models, where keys live in the customer's KMS or HSM and the provider cannot decrypt without them. Provider-managed default keys leave the provider able to decrypt. Disabling encryption fails the encryption requirement outright; IAM controls access but does not encrypt data. Placing keys in the provider's own internal key service still leaves the provider in control of the keys.

nodes.title: Network operations (CompTIA Network+): Key Ideas
nodes.content: Network+ tests operational fundamentals: how SNMP works for device monitoring, why baseline documentation matters, the change-management process that prevents accidental outages, and syslog severity levels that tell you how serious a message is. These appear in scenario questions where you're asked which tool to use or which process was skipped.

flashcards.front: SNMP — OID, MIB, community string, v2c vs v3.
flashcards.back: OID (Object Identifier): a dotted-number path in the MIB tree that uniquely identifies one piece of device data (e.g., `1.3.6.1.2.1.2.2.1.10` = ifInOctets). MIB (Management Information Base): the schema/dictionary that maps OIDs to human-readable names. Community string: a plain-text password used for SNMP v1/v2c authentication — typically 'public' (read) and 'private' (write); a well-known security weakness. SNMPv3 replaces community strings with proper user-based auth (MD5/SHA) and encryption (AES/DES).

flashcards.front: Why is network baseline documentation critical?
flashcards.back: A baseline records normal traffic volumes, CPU/memory levels, error rates, and routing tables — captured during a known-good period. When something goes wrong, you compare current readings to the baseline to spot the anomaly (utilization spiked 300%, a new route appeared, error rate tripled). Without a baseline, 'high CPU' is meaningless because you don't know what 'normal' was. Network+ expects you to identify baselining as a best practice before troubleshooting.

flashcards.front: Change management process — what are the key steps?
flashcards.back: Request change → assess risk and impact → obtain approval (CAB or manager) → schedule a maintenance window → implement → test and verify → document outcome → close. The exam distinguishes emergency changes (faster approval path for critical incidents) from standard changes (pre-approved, low-risk, routine). Skipping change management is the most common cause of self-inflicted outages.

0 Emergency, 1 Alert, 2 Critical, 3 Error, 4 Warning, 5 Notice, 6 Informational, 7 Debug. Lower number = more severe. Most organizations alert on 0–3 and log 0–6. Debug (7) produces enormous volume and is usually enabled only during active troubleshooting. The mnemonic: Every Awful Crisis Erodes Wisdom, No Debate.

questions.q: A cloud customer must permanently and verifiably render sensitive data unrecoverable at the Destroy phase, but the provider's multitenant storage means physical media destruction is not possible. Which technique is the recommended approach for cloud data destruction?
choices: Cryptographic erasure (cryptoshredding) — encrypt the data and then securely destroy the encryption keys so the ciphertext can never be decrypted
Degaussing the underlying drives — applying a strong magnetic field to the storage media to erase all residual data signals
Overwriting the logical volume once with zeros — a single pass that guarantees the original bits cannot be reconstructed on shared cloud hardware
Deleting the storage bucket through the console — removing the customer's pointer to the objects so the provider immediately reclaims and scrubs the media
questions.explanation: In multitenant cloud storage, customers cannot physically destroy shared media, so cryptographic erasure — encrypting data and then destroying the keys — is the recommended method: with the keys gone, the ciphertext is permanently unrecoverable. Degaussing requires physical access to the drives, which the tenant does not have. A single zero-overwrite pass cannot be assured on abstracted, replicated cloud storage. Simply deleting a bucket removes a reference but provides no verifiable guarantee the underlying data is irrecoverable.

questions.q: A SaaS provider is mapping out a structured set of secure development activities — threat modeling, secure coding, security testing, and review gates — to be embedded throughout how its software is built. Which CCSP concept does this describe?
choices: A configuration management database (CMDB), which inventories IT assets and their relationships to support change and incident management processes
A secure software development lifecycle (SDLC), which integrates security activities such as threat modeling, secure coding, and testing into each development phase
A business impact analysis (BIA), which identifies critical processes and the impact of their disruption to drive continuity planning priorities
A service level agreement (SLA), which defines measurable performance and availability commitments between the provider and its customers
questions.explanation: A secure SDLC embeds security activities — requirements, threat modeling, secure coding, security testing, and review gates — into every phase of software development, which is exactly what is described. A CMDB is an asset inventory database. A BIA is a continuity-planning analysis of disruption impact. An SLA is a contractual performance/availability commitment. Only the secure SDLC concerns building security into the development process itself.

questions.q: A cloud customer wants assurance that, if its provider ceases operations or it must change vendors, it can retrieve its data and avoid being technically locked into one provider's proprietary services. Which consideration MOST directly addresses this concern?
choices: Multi-factor authentication, ensuring that only authorized administrators can sign in to the provider's management console during the transition between vendors
Data dispersion, spreading encrypted data fragments across multiple storage nodes so that the loss of any single node does not compromise the data set
Resource pooling, allowing the provider to serve many tenants efficiently from a shared infrastructure base that lowers the customer's per-unit cost
Portability and vendor lock-in considerations, including exit-clause negotiation, data-extraction rights, and avoiding reliance on proprietary provider-specific features
questions.explanation: The ability to retrieve data and switch providers is governed by portability and vendor lock-in considerations — addressed through contractual exit clauses, guaranteed data-extraction rights and formats, and minimizing dependence on proprietary services. MFA controls administrative authentication, not portability. Data dispersion is a resiliency/availability technique within one provider. Resource pooling is a NIST cloud characteristic about multitenant efficiency, unrelated to exit and lock-in.

questions.q: A cloud operations team formalizes its IT service management so that proposed infrastructure changes are reviewed, approved, scheduled, and documented before deployment, reducing the chance that an unvetted change causes an outage. Which process does this describe?
choices: Problem management, which investigates the root cause of recurring incidents to prevent their future recurrence across the environment
Capacity management, which ensures sufficient compute, storage, and network resources are available to meet current and forecast demand
Change management, which reviews, approves, schedules, and documents modifications to the environment before they are implemented
Release management, which packages and version-controls software builds as they move from development toward production environments
questions.explanation: Change management is the ITSM discipline that controls modifications to the environment — requiring review, approval (often via a change advisory board), scheduling, and documentation before deployment to reduce change-induced outages. Problem management addresses the root cause of recurring incidents. Capacity management ensures adequate resources for demand. Release management packages and version-controls builds; while related, it does not perform the approval-and-authorization control that defines change management.
